unit.title: Global Challenges, Society and Sustainable Futures

theory.title: Bioethics, Science and Public Trust
theory.explanation: This C2 mission examines bioethics, science and public trust. Analyse competing interests, distinguish evidence from assumption and recognise how institutional choices distribute risks and benefits. Strong responses qualify claims, define terms precisely and acknowledge uncertainty without becoming evasive.
theory.tip: Name the mechanism, identify who benefits or bears the cost, and qualify conclusions in proportion to the evidence.

patterns.label: Define the issue
patterns.pattern: Specify the system, population and time frame under discussion.
examples: The proposed bioethics target applies to public buildings by 2035.

patterns.label: Interrogate evidence
patterns.pattern: Separate measured outcomes from projections and causal explanations.
examples: The association is consistent across districts, although it does not establish causation.

patterns.label: Map distribution
patterns.pattern: Ask how costs, access and risks differ across groups.
examples: The aggregate improvement conceals persistent gaps in peripheral neighbourhoods.

patterns.label: Recommend proportionately
patterns.pattern: Link an actionable recommendation to a measurable review point.
examples: The measure should be piloted, independently evaluated and revised after twelve months.

content.passage: A university research group faced criticism after announcing preliminary results from a small clinical study. The findings attracted extensive media coverage before the researchers had completed follow-up analysis. In response, the institution clarified the sample size, published its protocol and explained which outcomes remained uncertain. It also separated exploratory observations from pre-specified measures. The ethics committee noted that informed consent had been obtained, but argued that consent forms could not replace clear communication about the limits of the research. Public trust, the committee concluded, is strengthened when researchers disclose uncertainty and correct overstatement promptly. Replication and independent scrutiny were presented as normal components of scientific progress, not signs that the original team had failed.
